t: LeetCode 1501 — Countries You Can Safely Invest In
o: A person’s country is the 3-character prefix of their phone number, matched against Country.country_code. Crucially, every row of Calls contributes two data points: one call-end attributed to the caller’s country and one to the callee’s country — that is why Peru’s average in the example counts the 102- and 330-minute calls twice. We must report countries whose average over these attributed call-ends strictly exceeds the global average taken over all call-ends, which equals SUM(duration) / COUNT(*) over Calls alone (doubling scales numerator and denominator equally). In the sample the global average is 55.7 and only Peru (145.67) beats it.
k: Attribute each call to both endpoints by joining Person twice and taking SUBSTRING(phone_number, 1, 3) as the country code.
The global average over 2 x |Calls| entries is numerically identical to SUM(duration) / COUNT(*) computed directly on Calls.
The comparison is strict (>), and a country with zero attributed calls can never qualify.

a.n: Approach 1: Attribute Both Call Ends and Aggregate
a.i: Split every call into two records keyed by country code — one for the caller, one for the callee — then keep running sum and count per country alongside global totals. A final comparison emits the countries whose average is strictly above the global one. This is the imperative equivalent of the GROUP BY query and runs in a single pass over the data.
s: Map each person id to the 3-character prefix of phone_number.
For every call, add duration to the aggregates of both the caller’s and callee’s country, and to the global totals.
Compute globalAvg = totalSum / totalCount (each call counted twice, matching the attribution).
Return the names of countries whose average duration is strictly greater than globalAvg.

c.python:
import pandas as pd

def find_investments(person: pd.DataFrame, country: pd.DataFrame, calls: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    name_of = dict(zip(country['country_code'], country['name']))
    cc = person.set_index('id')['phone_number'].str.slice(0, 3)
    codes = pd.concat([cc.loc[calls['caller_id']], cc.loc[calls['callee_id']]], ignore_index=True)
    durs = pd.concat([calls['duration'], calls['duration']], ignore_index=True)
    df = pd.DataFrame({'code': codes, 'duration': durs})
    global_avg = df['duration'].mean()
    agg = df.groupby('code')['duration'].mean()
    res = agg[agg > global_avg].reset_index()
    res['country'] = res['code'].map(name_of)
    return res[['country']]

a.t: O(P + M) time — one pass over Person ids and Calls plus a pass over the per-country aggregates.
a.sp: O(P + G) — id-to-code map plus one aggregate entry per country that appears (G <= number of countries).

a.n: Approach 2: Pure SQL with UNION ALL and HAVING
a.i: The canonical database answer doubles the Calls table through a UNION ALL over joins on caller_id and callee_id, extracts each side’s country-code prefix, groups by country name, and filters with HAVING against a scalar subquery for the global average.
s: Join Calls to Person on caller_id and again on callee_id, projecting the phone prefix and duration; combine with UNION ALL.
Join the combined rows to Country on the prefix.
GROUP BY country name and compute AVG(duration).
Keep groups where AVG(duration) > (SELECT SUM(duration) / COUNT(*) FROM Calls).

w: In a database interview lead with the SQL query — it is the intended answer. Common pitfalls: attributing each call to only one endpoint, dividing by |Calls| instead of 2|Calls| when averaging the doubled rows (note the shortcut SUM/COUNT on the original table), using LEFT JOIN and letting countries with NULL averages through, and forgetting the strict inequality. Edge cases: duplicate Calls rows count every time, people calling within the same country contribute both ends there. Likely follow-ups: rank qualifying countries by average, or require a minimum call count via COUNT(*) in HAVING.
